'''Erich Rieger''' (1 October 1935 – 14 August 2021) was a German [[astrophysicist]] who spent his research career at the [[Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics]] (MPE) near [[Munich]]. He is notable for his 1984 discovery of the [[period (physics)|period]] of ~154 days in [[solar flares]].  Since the discovery, the period has been confirmed in most heliophysics data in the [[Solar System]], including the [[interplanetary magnetic field]], and has become known as the ''Rieger period'' (P<sub>R</sub>). Rieger died on 14 August 2021, at the age of 85.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Presse - Verein der Musikfreunde Gauting e.V. |url=https://www.musikfreunde-gauting.de/presse.html |access-date=2024-11-14 |website=www.musikfreunde-gauting.de}}</ref>

==Rieger periodicities==
===Rieger period===
Rieger and coworkers discovered in 1984 a strong period of ~154 days in hard solar flares, at least since the [[solar cycle 19]].<ref name="Rieger Share Forrest Kanbach 1984 pp. 623–625">{{cite journal | last1=Rieger | first1=E. | last2=Share | first2=G. H. | last3=Forrest | first3=D. J. | last4=Kanbach | first4=G. | last5=Reppin | first5=C. | last6=Chupp | first6=E. L. | title=A 154-day periodicity in the occurrence of hard solar flares? | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=312 | issue=5995 | year=1984 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/312623a0 | pages=623–625| bibcode=1984Natur.312..623R | s2cid=4348672 }}</ref> The period has since been confirmed in most heliophysics data and the [[interplanetary magnetic field]], and is commonly known as the ''Rieger period''.<ref name="Chowdhury Khan Ray pp. 1159–1180">{{cite journal | last1=Chowdhury | first1=Partha | last2=Khan | first2=Manoranjan | last3=Ray | first3=P.C. | title=Intermediate-term periodicities in sunspot areas during solar cycles 22 and 23 | journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society | publisher=Oxford University Press (OUP) | volume=392 | issue=1 | date=8 January 2009 | issn=0035-8711 | doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2008.14117.x | pages=1159–1180| bibcode=2009MNRAS.392.1159C | s2cid=121248083 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Rieger-type periodicities===
Besides numerous confirmations of P<sub>R</sub>, its [[resonance]] [[harmonics]] were reported as well, including {{fraction|5|6}}P<sub>R</sub>, {{fraction|2|3}}P<sub>R</sub>, {{fraction|1|2}}P<sub>R</sub>, {{fraction|1|3}}P<sub>R</sub>, and {{fraction|1|5}}P<sub>R</sub>, i.e., ~128, ~102, ~78, ~51, and ~31 days, called ''Rieger-type periodicities''.<ref name="Dimitropoulou Moussas Strintzi 2008 pp. 159–163">{{cite journal | last1=Dimitropoulou | first1=Michaila | last2=Moussas | first2=Xenophon | last3=Strintzi | first3=Dafni | title=Enhanced Rieger type periodicities' detection in X-ray solar flares and statistical validation of Rossby waves' existence | journal=Proceedings of the International Astronomical Union | publisher=Cambridge University Press (CUP) | volume=4 | issue=S257 | year=2008 | issn=1743-9213 | doi=10.1017/s1743921309029226 | pages=159–163| s2cid=122570191 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Types of data periodic with Rieger cycles include [[solar flare]]s, [[Photosphere|photospheric]] [[magnetic flux]], group [[sunspot number]]s, and [[proton]] speed.  Various longer (1–2 years) modulations also were reported in almost all heliophysics data types.  Besides the above mentioned, data types that exhibit long-periodic dynamics include solar flare index, [[Solar cycle#Solar radio flux|solar radio flux]], and others, except for the coronal index and 10.7 cm [[solar flux]].<ref name="Forgacs-Dajka Borkovits pp. 282–291">{{cite journal | last1=Forgacs-Dajka | first1=E. | last2=Borkovits | first2=T. | title=Searching for mid-term variations in different aspects of solar activity - looking for probable common origins and studying temporal variations of magnetic polarities | journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society | publisher=Oxford University Press (OUP) | volume=374 | issue=1 | date=1 January 2007 | issn=0035-8711 | doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2006.11167.x | pages=282–291| bibcode=2007MNRAS.374..282F | doi-access=free }}</ref>  

So far, these periodicities have been reported in different ranges, depending on data, location, epoch, and methodology, as 155–160 days, 160–165 days, 175–188 days, and 180–190 days.<ref name="Gurgenashvili Zaqarashvili Kukhianidze Oliver p=137">{{cite journal | last1=Gurgenashvili | first1=Eka | last2=Zaqarashvili | first2=Teimuraz V. | last3=Kukhianidze | first3=Vasil | last4=Oliver | first4=Ramon | last5=Ballester | first5=Jose Luis | last6=Dikpati | first6=Mausumi | last7=McIntosh | first7=Scott W. | title=North–South Asymmetry in Rieger-type Periodicity during Solar Cycles 19–23 | journal=The Astrophysical Journal | publisher=American Astronomical Society | volume=845 | issue=2 | date=18 August 2017 | issn=1538-4357 | doi=10.3847/1538-4357/aa830a | page=137| arxiv=1707.08615 | bibcode=2017ApJ...845..137G | s2cid=118807885 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Most of those studies indicate a leading periodicity ranging from 152 to 158 days, which appears to be dominant particularly in the time phase from ~1979–1983, corresponding to the [[solar maximum]] activity.<ref name="Chowdhury Kudela Moon pp. 581–602">{{cite journal | last1=Chowdhury | first1=Partha | last2=Kudela | first2=K. | last3=Moon | first3=Y.-J. | title=A Study of Heliospheric Modulation and Periodicities of Galactic Cosmic Rays During Cycle 24 | journal=Solar Physics | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=291 | issue=2 | date=7 January 2016 | issn=0038-0938 | doi=10.1007/s11207-015-0832-7 | pages=581–602| bibcode=2016SoPh..291..581C | s2cid=124226330 }}</ref>

===Origin of Rieger resonance===
Various proposals exist as to the origin of the underlying resonant process behind P<sub>R</sub> in the dynamics of Sun-ejected particles and its modulations and harmonics, including possible influences of planetary constellations on the Sun.<ref name="Kurochkin 1998 pp. 277–279">{{cite journal | last=Kurochkin | first=N. E. | title=Transient periodicity in solar activity | journal=Astronomical & Astrophysical Transactions | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=15 | issue=1–4 | year=1998 | issn=1055-6796 | doi=10.1080/10556799808201781 | pages=277–279| bibcode=1998A&AT...15..277K }}</ref><ref name="Abreu Beer Ferriz-Mas McCracken p=A88">{{cite journal | last1=Abreu | first1=J. A. | last2=Beer | first2=J. | last3=Ferriz-Mas | first3=A. | last4=McCracken | first4=K. G. | last5=Steinhilber | first5=F. | title=Is there a planetary influence on solar activity? | journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics | publisher=EDP Sciences | volume=548 | date=28 November 2012 | issn=0004-6361 | doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201219997 | page=A88| bibcode=2012A&A...548A..88A | doi-access=free | hdl=10261/421476 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> One such report found that a damped periodically forced nonlinear oscillator, which exhibits both periodic and chaotic behavior, can simulate the process described by Rieger periodicities.<ref name="Bai Cliver 1990 p=299">{{cite journal | last1=Bai | first1=Taeil | last2=Cliver | first2=E. W. | title=A 154 day periodicity in the occurrence rate of proton flares | journal=The Astrophysical Journal | publisher=American Astronomical Society | volume=363 | year=1990 | issn=0004-637X | doi=10.1086/169342 | page=299| bibcode=1990ApJ...363..299B }}</ref> The entire Rieger resonance was detected in the interplanetary magnetic field as well, including [[Earth]]'s vicinity.<ref name="Cane Richardson von Rosenvinge pp. 4437–4440">{{cite journal | last1=Cane | first1=H. V. | last2=Richardson | first2=I. G. | last3=von Rosenvinge | first3=T. T. | title=Interplanetary magnetic field periodicity of ~153 days | journal=Geophysical Research Letters | publisher=American Geophysical Union (AGU) | volume=25 | issue=24 | date=15 December 1998 | issn=0094-8276 | doi=10.1029/1998gl900208 | pages=4437–4440| bibcode=1998GeoRL..25.4437C | s2cid=121571473 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Other work==
===High-energy solar flares===
In 1989, Rieger provided strong evidence that flares with emissions >10 MeV are visible only near the [[solar limb]].<ref name="Vilmer pp. 3241–3268">{{cite journal | last=Vilmer | first=Nicole | title=Solar flares and energetic particles | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | publisher=The Royal Society | volume=370 | issue=1970 | date=13 July 2012 | issn=1364-503X | doi=10.1098/rsta.2012.0104 | pages=3241–3268| pmid=22665901 | bibcode=2012RSPTA.370.3241V | s2cid=9212696 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Gamma-ray-emitting flares are observed from sites located predominantly near the limb of the Sun; this effect was observed for flares detected at energies >0.3 MeV, but it is at energies >10 MeV that the effect is particularly pronounced.<ref>Ramaty, R., Simnett, G. M. (1991) Accelerated particles in solar flares. In: Sonett, C. P., Giampapa, M. S., Matthews, M. S. (Eds.) [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/#abs/1991suti.conf.....S/abstract The Sun in Time], The University of Arizona Press, Tucson, AZ, pp. 232–259.</ref> Since in both of these cases the bulk of the emission is [[bremsstrahlung]] from primary electrons, these results imply that the radiating electrons are [[Anisotropy energy|anisotropic]]. Thus, the anisotropy could result from the mirroring of the charged particles in the convergent chromospheric magnetic fields.

The emissions are strongly anisotropic, with more emission in the directions tangential to the [[photosphere]] than in directions away from the [[Sun]].<ref name="Miller Ramaty 1989 p=973">{{cite journal | last1=Miller | first1=James A. | last2=Ramaty | first2=Reuven | title=Relativistic electron transport and bremsstrahlung production in solar flares | journal=The Astrophysical Journal | publisher=American Astronomical Society | volume=344 | year=1989 | issn=0004-637X | doi=10.1086/167865 | page=973| bibcode=1989ApJ...344..973M }}</ref> In order to account for the anisotropy of the [[gamma-ray]] emission from high energy solar flares, invoked are electron transport in the [[Solar corona|coronal region]] and magnetic mirroring of converging magnetic flux tubes beneath the [[solar transition region]]. As the gaseous models of the Sun cannot support the existence of a real surface, another mechanism must act as a surface.

===Artificial comet===
Rieger was involved in the MPE early research initiatives, including the first [[Magnetosphere chronology|artificial comet]], created by a cloud of [[barium]] [[ion]]s, and which was released by the German IRM (Ion Release Module) satellite in 1985.<ref>Rieger, E. (2013) Explosive rocket men. In: [https://www.mpe.mpg.de/6652079/mpe-reflections-onlinepub-min.pdf Reflections on 50 years of extraterrestrial research, 1963–2013]. Monograph on the occasion of the golden jubilee of the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, pp. 18–21.</ref>
